Analysed Scores

Real pieces with expert Roman-numeral analyses under the notes, from the When in Rome corpus, one piece per page: Bach’s chorale “O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden” (“O Sacred Head, Now Wounded”) and the first movement of Beethoven’s “Moonlight” Sonata, and every example in Reger’s book of modulations. Play along with the analysis.

Real music, analysed by experts, with the Roman numerals under the notes where each chord begins. Each piece has its own page. The analyses come from When in Rome, a collection of harmonic analyses gathered by Mark Gotham and others.

The pieces

  • Bach: “O Haupt voll Blut und Wunden” (“O Sacred Head, Now Wounded”), a four-part chorale from the St Matthew Passion, analysed by Dmitri Tymoczko. Short, with a key change at nearly every phrase.
  • Beethoven: “Moonlight” Sonata, I, the whole first movement, analysed by Tsung-Ping Chen and Li Su. Slow harmony, the Neapolitan, a tour of keys, and the form part by part.
  • Reger: On the Theory of Modulation, all 100 short examples from Max Reger’s 1903 book of modulations, from one key to any other in a few chords, analysed by Néstor Nápoles López and others.
  • Modulation Finder: about 800 modulations in one list, sorted by the starting and ending key’s mode and the distance between them in half steps: the 200 textbook examples below, and short passages around the key changes in Bach’s chorales and 19th-century songs.
  • More modulation examples from harmony textbooks, also analysed by Nápoles López and others:
    • Rimsky-Korsakov: Practical Manual of Harmony, 37 short four-voice modulations from C major or A minor.
    • Tchaikovsky: Guide to the Practical Study of Harmony, 25 modulations from C major.
    • Aldwell and Schachter: Harmony and Voice Leading, seven examples: Bach chorales, Mozart and a progression.
    • Kostka and Payne: Tonal Harmony, 15 examples from Bach, Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Dvořák and Tchaikovsky.

Reading the labels

A key followed by a colon (d:) means the music has moved to that key (capital letter major, small letter minor); the numerals after it are in the new key. The figures are those of Chapter 16 (6, 64, 7, 65, 43, 42). ° is diminished and ø half-diminished, as in the book. V/iv and vii°7/V are the secondary chords of Chapters 17 and 18; N6 is the Neapolitan. A numeral sits under the bass where its chord starts; where the bass holds a note through a chord change, the note is written as tied notes so the label has a place (it sounds the same).

Using the scores

  • Play: Space plays and pauses. Click a note to move there.
  • Resizing: drag the line at the right edge of a score to make it wider or narrower (double-click it to reset); the bars re-flow to fit, and the size is kept for every score.
  • Keys: above a score, the key strip shows every key the analyst names, in order, as wide as the time spent there. Click a key to light its bars and hear them.
NoteFor teachers
  • Sources: the analyses are When in Rome’s RomanText files, CC BY-SA 4.0, shown as they are (signs written as in the book: ° ø, figures run together). The scores are Craig Sapp’s Humdrum encodings of public-domain editions, converted to ABC by scripts/when-in-rome/build.mjs. That script also places each numeral at its bar and beat, and the browser test checks every converted note against the original encoding.
  • One analysis per piece: the corpus has more than one analysis of both pieces (a second chorale analysis from the Bach Chorales Melody-Harmony Corpus, and Tymoczko’s Moonlight). The site shows one; build.mjs can show more, as tabs, by listing them in PIECES.
  • Notes and other readings: where an analyst left notes or alternative readings in the file, they are listed under the score.
  • Not edited: the analyses are not this site’s, and some labels follow the analyst’s conventions rather than the book’s (Cad64, Imaj7, I7).
  • More pieces: the corpus has hundreds more (all the Bach chorales, Beethoven’s sonatas and quartets, 19th-century songs). The same script can add them; each gets a page here.

For students

Aldwell, Edward, Carl Schachter, and Allen Cadwallader. Harmony and Voice Leading. Chapter 27, the source of the examples on the Aldwell and Schachter page. The dataset names the three authors but not the edition, which has not been checked.

Chen, Tsung-Ping, and Li Su. BPS-FH: Beethoven Piano Sonata with Functional Harmony dataset (ISMIR 2018). GitHub. github.com/Tsung-Ping/functional-harmony. The source of the Moonlight analysis, converted to RomanText and proof-read by Mark Gotham for When in Rome.

Gotham, Mark, et al. When in Rome: A Meta-Corpus of Functional Harmony. GitHub. github.com/MarkGotham/When-in-Rome. The analyses on this page (RomanText files), licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.

Kostka, Stefan, Dorothy Payne, and Byron Almén. Tonal Harmony. 8th ed., McGraw-Hill, 2018. Table of contents. highered.mheducation.com/sites/0078025141/information_center_view0/table_of_contents.html. Chapters 18 (Modulations Using Diatonic Common Chords) and 19 (Some Other Modulatory Techniques), the source of the examples on the Kostka and Payne page.

Reger, Max. Beiträge zur Modulationslehre. C. F. Kahnt Nachfolger, 1903. Translated by John Bernhoff as On the Theory of Modulation, Kahnt, [1904?]; reprinted as Supplement to the Theory of Modulation, Dover, 2007. The book whose 100 examples are shown on the Reger page. Public domain (Reger died in 1916).

Rimsky-Korsakov, Nikolay. Practical Manual of Harmony. A. Büttner, 1886. IMSLP. imslp.org/wiki/Practical_Manual_of_Harmony_(Rimsky-Korsakov,_Nikolay). The book whose modulation examples are on the Rimsky-Korsakov page; IMSLP has scans of later editions.

Tchaikovsky Research. “Guide to the Practical Study of Harmony.” en.tchaikovsky-research.net/pages/Guide_to_the_Practical_Study_of_Harmony. When and how Tchaikovsky wrote the book (1871, from his Moscow Conservatory lectures); Jurgenson, 1872; English translation by Emil Krall and James Liebling, 1900.

For teachers

Nápoles López, Néstor, et al. BCMH: The Bach Chorales Melody-Harmony Corpus. GitHub. github.com/napulen/BCMH. A second analysis of the chorale (automated translation to RomanText), not shown on the site.
